newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries ahead at midday, budget hopes help.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries ahead at midday, budget hopes help.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were at session highs at midday on Thursday, bouyed by hopes for a U.S. budget deal, coupon purchases by the Federal Reserve, and an unalarming reading on the nation's manufacturing sector.

"The Fed's coupon pass helped," said Bill Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist, referring to the Fed's purchases of coupons on Thursday morning. "I also think the purchasing managers' number was not alarming."
The 30-year Treasury bond was up 14/32 to 96-08, yielding 6.92 percent at midday.

The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) said its index edged down to 54.2 in April from 55.0 in March. The April reading reflected general strength in the economy, said Norbert Ore, chairman of the NAPM business survey committee, a condition that did not surprise the market.
Rumors of a nearing U.S. budget deal also helped bonds, participants said.
Speaking to reporters at the White House this morning, President Clinton hinted that the outlines of an agreement were taking shape.

"The market feels better and wants to trade higher," Hornbarger said. "All the numbers this week, if taken by themselves, say the Fed doesn't change monetary policy on May 20," he said, referring to a lower-than-forecast first-quarter Employment Cost Index and weaker-than-expected durable goods orders in February and March.

Traders said March personal income and spending data reported near the start of the trading session was market neutral. Personal income, up 0.6 percent in March, was a little higher than forecast. Personal spending, up 0.5 percent, matched economists' expectations.

A jump in new jobless claims for the week ended April 26 to 347,000 from a revised 319,000 a week earlier could have been positive for the market but was explained away as being related to auto industry strikes.
U.S. construction spending also slipped 0.2 percent, the government reported, a figure matching economists' forecasts.

While the market has made noticeable headway this week on economic data that was much less alarming than investors had feared, its upward climb has so far ground to a halt when the 30-year bond yield fell into the area between 6.92 percent and 6.93 percent.
That resistance could also be seen as the June bond contract rose to 109-25, its March 25 high, they said.
Analysts said it was unlikely that the market would pierce that area of resistance with the important April employment report coming on Friday.

The Labor Department's April employment report is not expected to be stronger than trend. Economists, on average, look for April payroll growth of 211,000 jobs with an unemployment rate stable at 5.2 percent, average hourly earnings up 0.3 percent and the workweek length shortened a bit to 34.7 hours in April from 34.8 hours in March.

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.10 percent, six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.31 percent and year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.56 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-7/32, yielding 6.26 percent. Five-year notes were up 3/32 to 100-10/32, yielding 6.55 percent. Ten-year notes were up 7/32 to 96-28/32, yielding 6.69 percent.
